newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH PM PARTY'S SUPPORT FLAT, BUT LEAD GROWS - POLL.
newsitem.headline: CZECH PM PARTY'S SUPPORT FLAT, BUT LEAD GROWS - POLL.

text.p: Support for Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) remained flat from December at 28 percent of potential voters, but the lead over its closest rival grew, a survey released on Monday showed.

The early January survey by the state research agency IVVM said the opposition centre-left Social Democrats (CSSD), led by parliamentary speaker Milos Zeman, dropped one percentage point in the the latest poll to 22 percent.

The junior coalition Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) gained one percentage point despite the December resignation of leader Jan Kalvoda from his justice minister and deputy premier posts after he admitted using an unattained title of "doctor of law".
IVVM said however the number of undecided voters, rose to 22 percent from 18 percent in December, and from 13 percent in November, indicating possible shifts ahead in the electorate.
"Such a strong proportion of undecided can signalise potential unrest and possible transfers (of voter preferences) in the next months," the survey's comments said.
Support for the third member of the coalition, the centrist Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL), remained flat from December at 11 percent.

The coalition lost its parliamentary majority in last June's elections, gaining 99 seats in the 200-seat chamber, but remained in power as the Social Democrats ruled out a grand coalition with the two extremist parties.
The January poll among 860 potential Czech voters also showed a large popularity drop for extremist parties, the ultra-right Republicans, and little-reformed Communists.
The Republicans, who got eight percent in the June elections, saw their support drop to just one percent in the January survey from four percent in December.
The IVVM said a statistical error could be behind the unusual drop, but added that it also may be a result of the party's lower exposition in media and public.
The hard-line Communists, who took 10.3 percent in the lower house elections, polled six percent, down from seven percent last month.
Sixty percent of the polled said they would vote in an election if it were held next week, 12 percent said they would "rather not", 19 percent said "definitely not", and nine percent were undecided.
The next general elections are scheduled for June, 2000.
